guide.title: Westport, Connecticut: From Onion Fields to an Arts Colony
guide.intro: Westport's story starts as "Green's Farm," named in 1732 for Bankside farmer John Green, after the area was briefly known as Bankside in 1693. Daniel Nash led 130 residents in petitioning Fairfield to protect their seaport's economic viability, and on May 28, 1835, Westport incorporated from lands taken from Fairfield, Weston, and Norwalk. The Revolution had already reached the shoreline: in April 1777, 1,850 British troops under Tryon landed at Compo Beach during the Danbury Raid, and Minutemen ambushed the column from the rear on its return, a stand the Minute Man statue still commemorates. By the 19th century, Westport was the leading onion-growing center in the United States until blight collapsed the industry and mills took its place. Around 1910, the town became a magnet for artists and writers, F. Scott Fitzgerald among them, a legacy carried on by residents Martha Stewart and, from 1960 until his 2008 death, Paul Newman.

sections.heading: From Bankside to an arts colony
sections.body: The area now known as Westport was briefly called Bankside in 1693, then officially named Green's Farm in 1732 in honor of Bankside farmer John Green. Daniel Nash led 130 residents in petitioning the Town of Fairfield to protect their seaport's economic viability, and on May 28, 1835, Westport incorporated from lands taken from Fairfield, Weston, and Norwalk. In April 1777, a British force of 1,850 troops under Major General William Tryon landed at Compo Beach during the Danbury Raid; local Minutemen ambushed the returning column from the rear, a stand the Minute Man statue commemorates today. By the 19th century Westport was the leading onion-growing center in the United States and a bustling Long Island Sound shipping center, until blight collapsed the onion industry and mills and factories replaced agriculture. Starting around 1910, Westport became a lively arts colony attracting artists, musicians, and writers — F. Scott Fitzgerald among them — a legacy carried forward by residents Martha Stewart and Paul Newman, who lived in town from 1960 until his death in 2008. Sherwood Island, whose first land the state acquired in 1914, became Connecticut's first state park after a 23-year battle with resisting landowners.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Drivers reach Westport via I-95 along the shoreline, the Merritt Parkway (Route 15) inland, or U.S. Route 1. Train travelers use Metro-North's New Haven Line, which has two stations in town — Westport (in the Saugatuck section, 1 Railroad Place) and Green's Farms — with direct service to Grand Central Terminal.

sections.heading: Stages, studios, and a shoreline park
sections.body: Sherwood Island State Park, Connecticut's first, spans 235 acres with a mile-long Long Island Sound beach, a seasonal nature center, disc golf, and the state's 9/11 Living Memorial. The Westport Country Playhouse presents mainstage productions, concerts, and its Barnstormer Series, while the Westport Museum for History and Culture tells the town's story, currently through "The Real Revolution," a 250th-anniversary exhibit. MoCA CT offers contemporary art exhibitions and a performing-arts season, and the Levitt Pavilion hosts free outdoor summer concerts on the riverside.

faq.question: How do I get to Westport?
faq.answer: Drivers use I-95, the Merritt Parkway (Route 15), or U.S. Route 1. Metro-North's New Haven Line stops at two in-town stations — Westport (Saugatuck) and Green's Farms — with direct service to Grand Central Terminal.

faq.question: What happened at Compo Beach in 1777?
faq.answer: During the April 1777 Danbury Raid, 1,850 British troops under Major General William Tryon landed at Compo Beach; local Minutemen ambushed the returning column from the rear, a stand the Minute Man statue commemorates.

faq.question: Is Sherwood Island really Connecticut's first state park?
faq.answer: Yes. The state acquired its first land there in 1914, though the park only fully opened to the public after a 23-year battle with resisting landowners.

faq.question: Is the Levitt Pavilion free?
faq.answer: Yes — its hallmark is free summer concert programming, supported by the CT Department of Economic and Community Development and the National Endowment for the Arts.

faq.question: Where can I stay in Westport?
faq.answer: The Inn at Longshore, a historic waterfront inn on the Longshore estate with fourteen rooms and the on-site restaurant La Plage, is Westport's verified in-town option.

places.summary: Connecticut's first state park, spanning 235 acres with a mile-long Long Island Sound beach, a seasonal nature center, disc golf, and the state's 9/11 Living Memorial. Open daily, 8 a.m. to sunset.

places.name: Westport Museum for History and Culture
places.summary: The town's history museum, currently presenting "The Real Revolution," an exhibit marking the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence through Revolutionary-era voices. Open Thursday-Saturday, 11 a.m.-5 p.m.

places.name: MoCA CT
places.summary: A contemporary art museum and cultural arts hub offering exhibitions, performing arts events, and education programs.

places.name: Levitt Pavilion for the Performing Arts
places.summary: An outdoor riverside venue whose hallmark is free summer concert programming, supported by the CT Department of Economic and Community Development and the National Endowment for the Arts.

places.name: Kawa Ni
places.summary: Chef Bill Taibe's playful Japanese izakaya-style pub in the Saugatuck neighborhood, focused on dumplings and noodle and rice bowls with whiskey, sake, and cocktails.

places.name: Gold's Delicatessen
places.summary: A Westport institution since 1958, this New York-style Jewish deli is known for house-made matzo ball soup, hand-sliced Nova lox, and fresh-roasted pastrami and corned beef.

places.name: Massi Co
places.summary: A Neapolitan-focused restaurant from AVPN-certified chef-owner Massimo, serving wood-fired Neapolitan-style pizzas and pastas rolled, cut, and shaped by hand daily.

places.name: The Inn at Longshore
places.summary: A historic waterfront inn on the Longshore estate between Long Island Sound and the Saugatuck River, with fourteen individually shaped rooms and the on-site restaurant La Plage.
